chapters.title: Chapter 1
paragraphs: During a recess in the Melvinski trial, in the big building that housed the Law Courts, the judges and the public prosecutor gathered in Ivan Egorovich Shebek's private room, and the talk drifted to the famous Krasovski case. Fedor Vasilievich argued heatedly that it fell outside their jurisdiction, Ivan Egorovich insisted it did not, and Peter Ivanovich, who had stayed out of the dispute from the start, took no part in it at all but leafed through a copy of the Gazette that had just been brought in.
"Gentlemen," he announced, "Ivan Ilych is dead!"
"No! Really?"

"Here, see for yourself," said Peter Ivanovich, passing Fedor Vasilievich the paper, still damp from the press. Inside a heavy black border ran the words: "Praskovya Fedorovna Golovina, with deep sorrow, announces to relatives and friends the death of her beloved husband Ivan Ilych Golovin, Member of the Court of Justice, who passed away on the fourth of February this year, 1882. The funeral will be held on Friday at one o'clock in the afternoon."

Ivan Ilych had been a colleague of the men in the room, and they had all been fond of him. He had been sick for some weeks with what was said to be an incurable illness. His position had been left open while he was away, though there had been quiet speculation that, if he died, Alexeev might step into the appointment, and that Vinnikov or Shtabel would then move up into Alexeev's place. So the very first thing each man in that private room thought, on hearing of Ivan Ilych's death, was what reshuffling and promotions it might bring about, for himself or for people he knew.

"This means I'm bound to get Shtabel's post, or Vinnikov's," thought Fedor Vasilievich. "It was promised to me ages ago, and the promotion is worth an extra eight hundred rubles a year, plus the allowance."

"Now I'll be able to put in for my brother-in-law's transfer from Kaluga," thought Peter Ivanovich. "My wife will be delighted, and then she can't keep saying I never do anything for her family." "I really thought he'd never get out of bed again," Peter Ivanovich said aloud. "It's very sad." "But what was actually wrong with him?"
"The doctors couldn't say—well, they could, but each of them said something different. The last time I saw him I thought he was on the mend."
"And I haven't been by to see him since the holidays. I kept meaning to go." "Did he leave any money?"
"I believe his wife had a little—but next to nothing."
"We'll have to call on her, of course, but they live such a dreadful distance away."
"A distance from you, you mean. Everything's a distance from your place."

"You see, he simply can't forgive me for living on the other side of the river," Peter Ivanovich said, smiling at Shebek. And so, still arguing about how far apart the different parts of town were, they all went back to the Court.

Quite apart from the calculations about transfers and promotions that the death might set in motion, the bare fact that a close acquaintance had died stirred in everyone who heard of it, as it always does, a smug little sense of relief: "It's him who's dead, not me."

Each of them thought, or felt, "Well, he's gone, but here I am, alive!" Still, the closer acquaintances—the ones who counted as Ivan Ilych's friends—could not help reflecting that they would now have to go through the tiresome motions that decency required: attending the funeral service and paying a visit of condolence to the widow.

Fedor Vasilievich and Peter Ivanovich had been his closest acquaintances. Peter Ivanovich had studied law alongside Ivan Ilych and felt he owed him something. Having mentioned Ivan Ilych's death to his wife over dinner, along with his hopes of getting her brother transferred to their district, Peter Ivanovich gave up his usual afternoon nap, put on his evening clothes, and drove to Ivan Ilych's house.

A carriage and two cabs stood at the door. Downstairs in the front hall, leaning against the wall beside the coat-stand, was a coffin lid, draped in cloth of gold and trimmed with gold braid and tassels, freshly buffed with metal polish. Two ladies in black were removing their fur cloaks. One of them Peter Ivanovich recognized as Ivan Ilych's sister; the other was a stranger to him. His colleague Schwartz was just coming down the stairs, but on seeing Peter Ivanovich come in he stopped and gave him a wink, as though to say, "Ivan Ilych has bungled the whole business—not the way you and I would have managed it."

Schwartz, with his Piccadilly side-whiskers and his lean figure in evening dress, wore his usual look of elegant gravity, which clashed with his actual playfulness of character and seemed especially pointed here—or so it struck Peter Ivanovich.

Peter Ivanovich let the ladies go ahead of him and followed slowly up the stairs. Schwartz did not come down but stayed put, and Peter Ivanovich understood that he wanted to settle where they would play bridge that evening. The ladies went up to the widow's room, while Schwartz, his lips pressed gravely together but his eyes still amused, indicated with a flick of his eyebrows the room to the right, where the body lay.

Peter Ivanovich went in, as everyone does on such occasions, unsure of what he was supposed to do. The one thing he knew was that at moments like this it never hurts to cross oneself. He was less sure whether one should bow at the same time. So he split the difference. As he entered, he started crossing himself and added a slight motion that might pass for a bow. At the same time, as far as the movement of his head and arm would let him, he took in the room. Two young men—nephews, by the look of them, one a high-school student—were on their way out, crossing themselves as they went. An old woman stood perfectly still, and beside her a lady with strangely arched eyebrows was murmuring something to her in a whisper. A hearty, brisk Church Reader, in a frock coat, was reading aloud in a tone that left no room for argument. The butler's assistant, Gerasim, stepped lightly past Peter Ivanovich, scattering something across the floor. Catching sight of this, Peter Ivanovich at once became aware of a faint smell of a body beginning to decay.

On his last visit to Ivan Ilych, Peter Ivanovich had seen Gerasim in the study. Ivan Ilych had been very fond of him, and the man had taken on the work of a sick-nurse. Peter Ivanovich went on crossing himself and bowing his head slightly in a direction that fell somewhere between the coffin, the Reader, and the icons set out on a table in the corner. Then, when it seemed to him that he had been crossing himself for rather too long, he stopped and turned to look at the body.

The dead man lay, as the dead always do, with that peculiar heaviness, his stiff limbs sunk into the soft padding of the coffin, his head bowed forever on the pillow. His brow, yellow and waxen, with bald patches above the hollowed temples, jutted up in the way that only the dead do, and his nose stood out as if pressing down on his upper lip. He had changed a great deal and grown even thinner since Peter Ivanovich had last seen him, yet, as is always true of the dead, his face looked handsomer and, above all, more dignified than it had in life. The expression on it seemed to say that whatever had to be done had been done, and done right. There was also, in that expression, a reproach and a warning to the living. Peter Ivanovich felt the warning was out of place—or at any rate had nothing to do with him. He felt a vague discomfort, and so he hurriedly crossed himself again, turned, and walked out the door—rather too quickly and with rather too little regard for propriety, as he himself was aware.

Schwartz was waiting for him in the next room, his legs planted wide apart, both hands fiddling behind his back with the top hat he held there. The mere sight of that playful, well-groomed, elegant figure was a relief to Peter Ivanovich. He felt that Schwartz stood above all this business and would not let any of it drag him down. His very look said that this little episode—a church service for Ivan Ilych—was certainly no reason to disrupt the routine of the evening: in other words, nothing would stop him that night from breaking the seal on a fresh pack of cards and shuffling them while a footman set out new candles; there was no reason to think this whole affair would prevent them from passing a pleasant evening. Indeed, he said as much in a whisper as Peter Ivanovich went past, suggesting they meet for a game at Fedor Vasilievich's. But it seemed Peter Ivanovich was not fated to play bridge that evening. Praskovya Fedorovna—a short, stout woman who, for all her efforts to the contrary, had kept steadily widening from the shoulders down, and who had the very same oddly arched eyebrows as the lady standing by the coffin—came out of her room, dressed entirely in black, her head draped in lace, accompanied by some other ladies. She led them to the room where the body lay and said, "The service is about to begin. Please go in."

Schwartz made a vague bow and stood where he was, plainly neither accepting nor refusing the invitation. Praskovya Fedorovna, recognizing Peter Ivanovich, sighed, came right up to him, took his hand, and said, "I know you were a true friend to Ivan Ilych..." Then she looked at him, waiting for the appropriate reply. And Peter Ivanovich knew that, just as crossing oneself had been the correct thing to do in that other room, the correct thing here was to squeeze her hand, sigh, and say, "Believe me..." So he did all of it, and as he did, he felt that the intended effect had been produced: both he and she were moved.

"Come with me. I'd like to speak to you before it starts," said the widow. "Give me your arm." Peter Ivanovich offered his arm, and they went off toward the inner rooms, passing Schwartz, who gave Peter Ivanovich a sympathetic wink.
"So much for our bridge! Don't mind if we bring in another player. Maybe you can join in once you've made your escape," said his playful look.

Peter Ivanovich sighed even more deeply and mournfully, and Praskovya Fedorovna gave his arm a grateful press. When they reached the drawing room, which was upholstered in pink cretonne and lit by a single dim lamp, they sat down at the table—she on a sofa, Peter Ivanovich on a low ottoman whose springs gave way under him in fits and jerks. Praskovya Fedorovna had been about to warn him to take another seat, but felt that such a warning was hardly in keeping with her present grief, and thought better of it. As he sank onto the ottoman, Peter Ivanovich remembered how Ivan Ilych had decorated this room and had consulted him about this very pink cretonne with its green leaves. The room was crowded with furniture and little ornaments, and as the widow crossed to the sofa, the lace of her black shawl snagged on the edge of the table. Peter Ivanovich rose to free it, and the springs of the ottoman, released from his weight, sprang up and gave him a shove. The widow began working at the shawl herself, so Peter Ivanovich sat down again, pinning the rebellious springs beneath him. But she had not quite gotten it loose, so he stood up once more, and once more the ottoman revolted, this time even creaking. When it was finally over, she took out a clean cambric handkerchief and began to weep. The whole episode with the shawl and the struggle with the ottoman had cooled Peter Ivanovich's feelings, and he sat there looking sullen. The awkwardness was broken by Sokolov, Ivan Ilych's butler, who came in to report that the burial plot Praskovya Fedorovna had picked out would cost two hundred rubles. She stopped crying, looked at Peter Ivanovich with the air of a martyr, and remarked in French how very hard it all was for her. Peter Ivanovich made a wordless gesture meant to convey his complete conviction that it must indeed be so. "Please, smoke," she said in a tone both generous and crushed, and turned to discuss with Sokolov the price of the grave.

As he lit his cigarette, Peter Ivanovich heard her inquire in minute detail into the prices of the various plots in the cemetery before finally settling on the one she would take. That done, she gave instructions about hiring the choir, and Sokolov left the room. "I see to everything myself," she told Peter Ivanovich, moving aside the albums that lay on the table; and noticing that his cigarette ash threatened it, she at once handed him an ashtray, saying as she did, "I think it's mere affectation to claim that grief keeps one from attending to practical matters. Quite the opposite—if anything can, I won't say console me, but at least distract me, it's seeing to everything that concerns him." Again she took out her handkerchief, as if about to cry, but then, as though catching hold of herself, she gave a little shake and began to speak calmly. "But there's something I wanted to discuss with you."
Peter Ivanovich bowed, keeping a firm grip on the springs of the ottoman, which had at once begun to twitch beneath him.
"He suffered terribly the last few days."
"Did he?" said Peter Ivanovich.

"Oh, terribly! He screamed without stopping—not for minutes but for hours. For the last three days he screamed nonstop. It was beyond bearing. I don't know how I survived it; you could hear him three rooms away. Oh, what I've been through!"
"Was he really conscious through all of it?" Peter Ivanovich asked.
"Yes," she whispered. "To the very end. He said goodbye to us a quarter of an hour before he died, and asked us to take Vasya out of the room."

The thought of this man's suffering—a man he had known so intimately, first as a cheerful little boy, then as a schoolmate, and later as a grown colleague—suddenly filled Peter Ivanovich with horror, despite his uneasy awareness of the play-acting going on between himself and this woman. Once more he saw that brow, and that nose pressing down on the lip, and he was afraid for himself.

"Three days of agony, and then death! Why, that could come for me too, suddenly, at any moment," he thought, and for an instant he was terrified. But then—he could not have said how—the familiar reassurance rose up at once: that this had happened to Ivan Ilych and not to him, that it neither should nor could happen to him, and that to imagine it could would be to give in to gloom, which he had no business doing, as Schwartz's face made perfectly plain. Having thought this through, Peter Ivanovich felt steadier, and began to ask, with real interest, about the details of Ivan Ilych's death, as though death were some mishap peculiar to Ivan Ilych but certainly not to himself. After a good many details about the genuinely dreadful physical agonies Ivan Ilych had endured—details he gathered only from the effect those agonies had had on Praskovya Fedorovna's nerves—the widow evidently decided it was time to get down to business.

"Oh, Peter Ivanovich, how hard it is! How terribly, terribly hard!" And she began to cry again. Peter Ivanovich sighed and waited for her to finish blowing her nose. When she had, he said, "Believe me..." and she started talking once more, coming out at last with what was clearly her real reason for wanting him: to ask how she might secure a grant of money from the government on account of her husband's death. She made it look as though she were asking Peter Ivanovich's advice about her pension, but he soon saw that she already knew the matter inside and out, down to the last detail—more, in fact, than he did. She knew exactly how much could be wrung out of the government because of her husband's death; what she wanted was to find out whether she might somehow squeeze out more. Peter Ivanovich tried to think of a way, but after pondering it for a while and, for form's sake, condemning the government's stinginess, he said he doubted anything further could be gotten. At that she sighed and plainly began casting about for a way to be rid of her visitor. Sensing this, he stubbed out his cigarette, rose, pressed her hand, and went out into the front hall. In the dining room—where the clock Ivan Ilych had so loved and bought at an antique shop was standing—Peter Ivanovich came upon a priest and a few acquaintances who had arrived for the service, and there he recognized Ivan Ilych's daughter, a handsome young woman. She was in black, and her slim figure looked slimmer than ever. Her expression was somber, hard, almost angry, and she bowed to Peter Ivanovich as though he were somehow to blame. Just behind her, wearing the same offended look, stood a wealthy young man—an examining magistrate Peter Ivanovich also knew, and, as he had heard, her fiancé. He bowed to them mournfully and was about to go through into the death chamber when, from under the staircase, out came Ivan Ilych's schoolboy son, who looked remarkably like his father. He was a little Ivan Ilych, just as Peter Ivanovich remembered him from their student days. The boy's eyes were red from crying, and in them was the look you see in the eyes of boys of thirteen or fourteen who are no longer innocent. Catching sight of Peter Ivanovich, he scowled in shame and gloom. Peter Ivanovich gave him a nod and went into the death chamber. The service began: candles, groaning, incense, tears, sobs. Peter Ivanovich stood staring grimly down at his own feet. He never once looked at the dead man, refused to let himself be dragged down by any of it, and was among the first to leave the room. There was no one in the front hall, but Gerasim came darting out of the dead man's room, rummaged through the fur coats with his strong hands to find Peter Ivanovich's, and helped him into it.

"Well, Gerasim, old fellow," said Peter Ivanovich, just to say something. "A sad business, isn't it?" "It's God's will. We'll all come to it in the end," said Gerasim, showing his teeth—the even, white teeth of a healthy peasant—and then, like a man up to his neck in urgent work, he briskly threw open the front door, called the coachman, helped Peter Ivanovich into the sledge, and sprang back to the porch as if already poised for whatever came next. Peter Ivanovich found the fresh air especially welcome after the smell of incense, the corpse, and carbolic acid.
"Where to, sir?" asked the coachman.
"It's not too late even now.... I'll stop by Fedor Vasilievich's."
So he drove there and found them just finishing the first rubber, so it was very easy for him to take a hand.

chapters.title: Chapter 2
paragraphs: Ivan Ilych's life had been the most simple, the most ordinary—and therefore the most appalling. He had been a Member of the Court of Justice, and he died at forty-five. His father had been a government official who, after serving in various ministries and departments in Petersburg, had built the kind of career that lands men in posts they cannot be removed from on account of their long service, even though they are plainly unfit for any real responsibility—posts that are therefore invented specially for them, fictitious in everything but the salaries of six to ten thousand rubles, which are not fictitious at all, and on which such men go on living to a ripe old age. Such was Ilya Epimovich Golovin, Privy Councillor and superfluous member of a number of superfluous institutions.

He had three sons, of whom Ivan Ilych was the second. The eldest had taken the same path as his father, only in a different department, and was already nearing the point in his service where a similar sinecure would fall into his lap. The third son was a failure. He had wrecked his prospects in a string of positions and was now working in the railway department. His father and brothers—and even more so their wives—not only disliked running into him but did their best to forget he existed unless they were forced to remember. His sister had married Baron Greff, a Petersburg official cut from their father's cloth. Ivan Ilych was, as people said, le phénix de la famille—the family's shining exception. He was neither as chilly and stiff as his elder brother nor as wild as the younger, but struck a happy balance between them: intelligent, polished, lively, and easy to like. He had studied at the School of Law alongside his younger brother, who failed to finish and was thrown out in the fifth class; Ivan Ilych completed the course well. Even at the School of Law he was already what he would remain for the rest of his life: capable, cheerful, good-natured, sociable, yet strict in carrying out what he took to be his duty—and what he took to be his duty was whatever those in authority took to be his duty. He was no toady, as boy or man, but from his earliest youth he was drawn, by his very nature, to people of high rank the way a fly is drawn to light, taking on their manners and their views of life and cultivating friendships with them. All the enthusiasms of his childhood and youth passed through him without leaving much of a mark; he gave himself over to sensuality and vanity, and, in his later years among the upper classes, to liberalism—but always within the limits his instinct unfailingly pointed out to him as the proper ones.

At school he had done things that had once struck him as shameful and had filled him with self-disgust at the time; but later, when he saw that people of good standing did the same things and felt no guilt about them, he managed—not exactly to call them right, but to forget about them altogether, or at least to feel no twinge when they came to mind. Having graduated from the School of Law and qualified for the tenth rank in the civil service, and having gotten money from his father for his outfit, Ivan Ilych ordered his clothes from Scharmer, the fashionable tailor, hung a little medallion engraved respice finem on his watch chain, said goodbye to his professor and to the prince who was the school's patron, gave a farewell dinner with his classmates at Donon's first-class restaurant, and—with his new and fashionable trunk, his linen, clothes, shaving things and other toiletries, and a travelling rug, all bought at the best shops—set off for one of the provinces, where, through his father's connections, he had been attached to the governor as an official for special assignments.

In the province, Ivan Ilych quickly set up a position for himself as easy and agreeable as the one he had enjoyed at the School of Law. He did his official work, advanced his career, and at the same time amused himself pleasantly and with proper decorum. Now and then he made official trips to the rural districts, where he carried himself with dignity toward superiors and subordinates alike, and discharged the tasks entrusted to him—chiefly those concerning the religious sectarians—with a precision and incorruptible honesty he could not help feeling proud of.

In his official work, despite his youth and his taste for lighthearted fun, he was remarkably reserved, exacting, even severe; but in society he was often amusing and witty, always good-natured, faultless in his manners, and bon enfant, as the governor and his wife—who treated him almost as one of the family—used to say of him.

In the province he had an affair with a lady who set her cap at the dashing young lawyer, and there was a milliner too; and there were drinking parties with visiting aides-de-camp, and late-night trips to a certain street of dubious reputation on the edge of town; and there was a fair amount of fawning on his chief and even on his chief's wife—but all of it carried such an air of good breeding that no harsh name could be pinned on it. It all fell neatly under the French phrase "Il faut que jeunesse se passe"—youth must have its fling. It was all done with clean hands, in clean linen, in French phrases, and, above all, among people of the very best society, and therefore with the blessing of people of rank.

So Ivan Ilych served for five years, and then his official life took a turn. The new, reformed judicial institutions were established, and new men were wanted. Ivan Ilych became one of those new men. He was offered the post of examining magistrate and took it, even though it was in another province and meant giving up the connections he had built and starting over with new ones. His friends gathered to see him off; they had a group photograph taken, presented him with a silver cigarette case, and he set out for his new post.

As an examining magistrate, Ivan Ilych was just as comme il faut and just as decorous a man—commanding general respect and able to keep his official duties apart from his private life—as he had been when serving on special assignments. But his work as examining magistrate was far more interesting and appealing than before. In his earlier post it had been pleasant to wear an undress uniform tailored by Scharmer and to walk past the crowd of petitioners and officials anxiously waiting for an audience with the governor, who envied him as he strolled, free and easy, straight into his chief's private room for a cup of tea and a cigarette. But back then few people were directly answerable to him—only police officials and the sectarians when he went out on special missions—and he liked to treat them courteously, almost as equals, as if to let them feel that the very man who had the power to crush them was treating them in this simple, friendly way. There were not many such people then. But now, as an examining magistrate, Ivan Ilych felt that everyone, without exception—even the most important and self-satisfied—was in his hands. He had only to write a few words on a sheet of paper bearing a certain heading, and this or that important, self-satisfied person would be hauled before him as a defendant or a witness, and if Ivan Ilych chose not to let him sit, the man would have to stand and answer his questions. Ivan Ilych never abused this power; on the contrary, he tried to soften how it showed. But it was the awareness of that power, and of his own ability to soften its effect, that gave his office its chief interest and appeal. In the work itself, and especially in his examinations, he very quickly developed a knack for stripping away everything irrelevant to the legal side of a case and reducing even the most tangled matter to a form that could be set down on paper purely in its externals—keeping his own opinion of it out of it entirely—while above all observing every required formality. The work was new, and Ivan Ilych was one of the first men to apply the new Code of 1864.

On taking up the post of examining magistrate in a new town, he formed new acquaintances and connections, set himself up on a new footing, and adopted a somewhat different manner. Toward the provincial authorities he took an attitude of dignified aloofness, but he singled out the best circle of legal men and well-off gentry living in town and assumed a tone of mild disgruntlement with the government, of moderate liberalism, of enlightened civic-mindedness. At the same time, without changing the elegance of his dress in the slightest, he stopped shaving his chin and let his beard grow as it would.

Ivan Ilych settled into this new town very comfortably. The local society, which leaned toward opposition to the governor, was friendly; his salary was larger; and he took up the game of vint, which he found added a good deal to the pleasures of life, for he had a head for cards, played good-humoredly, and reckoned quickly and shrewdly, so that he usually came out ahead.

After two years there he met his future wife, Praskovya Fedorovna Mikhel, the most attractive, clever, and dazzling girl in the set he moved in, and—among his other amusements and respites from the labors of an examining magistrate—Ivan Ilych struck up a light, playful relationship with her.

While serving on special assignments he had been in the habit of dancing, but now, as an examining magistrate, it was something he did only rarely. When he did dance these days, it was as if to show that, although he served under the reformed order of things and had reached the fifth official rank, he could still, when it came to dancing, do it better than most. So at the close of an evening he would sometimes dance with Praskovya Fedorovna, and it was chiefly during these dances that he won her over. She fell in love with him. At first Ivan Ilych had no firm intention of marrying, but once the girl had fallen for him, he said to himself, "Really, why shouldn't I marry?"

Praskovya Fedorovna came of a good family, was not bad-looking, and had a little property of her own. Ivan Ilych might have aimed at a more brilliant match, but even this was a good one. He had his salary, and she, he hoped, would have an income to match. She was well connected, and she was a sweet, pretty, thoroughly proper young woman. To say that Ivan Ilych married because he had fallen in love with Praskovya Fedorovna and found that she shared his views of life would be just as wrong as to say he married because his social circle approved of the match. He was moved by both: the marriage brought him personal satisfaction, and at the same time it was regarded as the right thing to do by the most highly placed of his associates. So Ivan Ilych got married.

The wedding preparations and the start of married life—the marital tenderness, the new furniture, new dishes, new linen—were all very pleasant, right up until his wife became pregnant. By then Ivan Ilych had begun to think that marriage would not spoil the easy, agreeable, lighthearted, and always decorous character of his life—a life society approved of and he regarded as the natural order of things—but might even improve it. From the very first months of his wife's pregnancy, however, something new appeared, something unpleasant, oppressive, and unseemly that there was no escaping. Without any reason—de gaieté de coeur, as Ivan Ilych put it to himself—his wife began to disturb the pleasantness and propriety of their life. She grew jealous for no cause, demanded that he devote his whole attention to her, found fault with everything, and made coarse, ill-mannered scenes.

At first Ivan Ilych hoped to slip free of this unpleasant state of affairs by means of the same easy, decorous attitude toward life that had always served him: he tried to ignore his wife's bad moods, went on living in his usual easy and pleasant way, invited friends over for cards, and tried as well going off to his club or spending his evenings with friends. But one day his wife laid into him so fiercely, with such coarse language, and kept abusing him every time he failed to meet her demands, so doggedly and with such evident resolve not to relent until he gave in—that is, until he stayed home and was as bored as she was—that he took alarm. He saw now that married life, at least with Praskovya Fedorovna, was not always conducive to the comforts and pleasures of life, but on the contrary often violated both ease and decorum, and that he therefore had to fortify himself against such violations. So Ivan Ilych set about finding the means to do it. His official work was the one thing that impressed Praskovya Fedorovna, and through his work and the duties tied to it, he began doing battle with his wife to secure his own independence.

With the birth of their child, and the attempts to feed it, and the various failures in doing so, and the real and imagined ailments of mother and baby—matters in which his sympathy was demanded but which he understood nothing about—the need to carve out for himself an existence apart from his family grew still more pressing.

As his wife grew more irritable and demanding, Ivan Ilych shifted the center of gravity of his life more and more onto his work, and the more he did so, the more he came to enjoy that work and the more ambitious he became.

Very soon—within a year of the wedding—Ivan Ilych had realized that marriage, while it may add certain comforts to life, is in fact a complicated and difficult business, and that to do one's duty by it—that is, to lead the decorous life society approves of—one has to take up a definite attitude toward it, exactly as one does toward one's official duties.

And such an attitude toward married life Ivan Ilych worked out. From it he asked only those conveniences—dinner at home, a wife to keep the house, a bed—that it could supply, and, above all, that outward propriety which public opinion required. For the rest, he looked for lightheartedness and decorum, and was very grateful when he found them; but if he met with hostility and complaint, he withdrew at once into his own fenced-off world of official duties, where he found his satisfaction.

Ivan Ilych was regarded as a good official, and after three years he was made Assistant Public Prosecutor. His new duties—their importance, the power to indict and imprison anyone he chose, the publicity his speeches received, and the success he enjoyed in all of it—made his work more appealing than ever.

More children came along. His wife grew more and more peevish and bad-tempered, but the attitude Ivan Ilych had adopted toward home life made him nearly impervious to her grumbling. After seven years' service in that town, he was transferred to another province as Public Prosecutor. They moved, but money was short, and his wife disliked the place they had moved to. Although the salary was higher, the cost of living was higher too; on top of that, two of their children died, and family life became even more disagreeable to him.

Praskovya Fedorovna blamed her husband for every inconvenience they ran into in their new home. Most of the conversations between husband and wife, especially about the children's education, led back to subjects that revived old quarrels, and those quarrels were liable to flare up again at any moment. All that remained were those rare spells of tenderness that still came to them now and then but never lasted long. They were little islands where the couple dropped anchor for a while before setting out again onto that ocean of unspoken hostility, which showed itself in how distant they kept from each other. This distance might have grieved Ivan Ilych had he believed it ought not to exist; but he had come to regard the situation as normal, and even made it the goal he aimed at in family life. His aim was to free himself, more and more, from these unpleasantnesses, and to give them an appearance of harmlessness and propriety. He managed this by spending less and less time with his family, and when he had to be at home, he protected his position by surrounding himself with outsiders. The main thing, though, was that he had his official duties. The whole interest of his life now centered on the official world, and that interest absorbed him completely. The awareness of his power—the power to ruin anyone he wished to ruin—the importance, the very outward dignity of his entrance into court, of his meetings with subordinates, his success with superiors and inferiors alike, and above all his masterly handling of cases, of which he was well aware—all of this gave him pleasure and filled his life, along with chats with his colleagues, dinners, and bridge. So on the whole Ivan Ilych's life went on flowing exactly as he believed it should—pleasantly and properly.

Things went on this way for another seven years. By then his eldest daughter was sixteen, another child had died, and only one son was left—a schoolboy who was himself a bone of contention. Ivan Ilych wanted to send him to the School of Law, but out of spite Praskovya Fedorovna enrolled him in the High School. The daughter had been educated at home and had turned out well; the boy was not a poor student either.
